blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: No guide of yours covers this subject, so this part was written for the site, as of October 2026. Frontend libraries change quickly: check the official documentation before relying on a detail.

### The rules of hooks

React tracks hooks by **call order**, in a list for each component. So:

1. Call hooks only at the top level, never inside conditions, loops or nested functions.
2. Call them only from components or custom hooks.

blocks.title: Why order matters

blocks.text:
If the order changes between renders, React gives each hook the wrong slot. The ESLint plugin `react-hooks` catches this, so keep it enabled.

### useState details

blocks.code: const [draft, setDraft] = useState(() => localStorage.getItem('draft') ?? '');
blocks.title: Lazy initial state

blocks.text:
Passing a function means that the costly read runs once only. A value expression would run on every render, and its result would then be ignored.

| Choose | When |
|---|---|
| One object in state | Fields that change together |
| Several `useState`s | Unrelated values |
| `useReducer` | Many transitions, or next state depends on several fields |

### useRef

A ref is a box whose `.current` survives renders, and changing it doesn't cause a render.

blocks.title: Two main uses

blocks.text:
| | `useState` | `useRef` |
|---|---|---|
| Causes a render when changed | Yes | No |
| Value during render | A snapshot | Latest, but don't read it in render |
| Use for | What's shown | Timers, DOM nodes, previous values |

Don't read or write `ref.current` during rendering, except for lazy initialisation, because it makes rendering impure.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Hooks rely on call order
- Lazy initial state for costly work
- A ref survives renders silently
- Use state for anything displayed

`useEffect` synchronises a component with something **outside React**: the network, timers, subscriptions and the DOM. It's the most misused hook.

### How it runs

blocks.code:
sequenceDiagram
  participant R as React
  participant E as Effect
  R->>R: render and commit to the DOM
  R->>E: run effect (first time)
  R->>R: dependencies change: render and commit
  R->>E: run cleanup of the previous effect
  R->>E: run the new effect
  R->>R: component unmounts
  R->>E: run the last cleanup
blocks.title: The life of an effect
A subscription with cleanup

blocks.text:
| Dependencies | Runs |
|---|---|
| `[a, b]` | After mount, and when a or b changes |
| `[]` | After mount only |
| Missing | After every render |

### You might not need an effect

Most bugs come from effects that shouldn't exist.

| Instead of an effect for | Do this |
|---|---|
| Calculating derived data | Compute during render |
| Costly calculation | `useMemo` |
| Reacting to a click | Put it in the event handler |
| Resetting state when a prop changes | A `key` |
| Fetching data | A data library such as TanStack Query |
| Notifying a parent | Call its function in the handler |

blocks.title: An effect that shouldn't exist

blocks.text:
The test: **why does this code run?** Because the component appeared or data changed: an effect may fit. Because a user clicked: use the handler.

### Fetching with an effect, correctly

It's useful to see the problems, even if you'll generally use a library.

blocks.title: Handling races and cancellation

blocks.text:
Without the abort, if `id` changes from 1 to 2 and request 1 responds last, the page shows the wrong order. This code still has no caching, retries or sharing between components, which is why libraries exist.

### Dependencies are not a choice

Include every reactive value that the effect uses. Don't silence the lint rule. If a dependency causes too many runs, fix the cause:

| Problem | Fix |
|---|---|
| An object made in render changes each time | Move it inside the effect, or use primitive values |
| A function prop changes each render | `useCallback` in the parent, or move it inside |
| State only used for its previous value | Use the updater form |

### The stale closure

blocks.title: A timer stuck at 1

blocks.text:
The effect's closure captured the first render's `count`. It stays at 1. Fix it with `setCount((c) => c + 1)`, which needs no captured value.

### Double runs in development

Strict Mode runs effects, cleans them up, and runs them again on mount, in development only. This proves that your cleanup works. If this breaks something, your effect has a bug, such as a missing cleanup.

**"What is the stale closure problem?"** A function captures variables from the render that created it. If an effect with empty dependencies uses state, it sees the initial value forever. Fix it with an updater, correct dependencies, or a ref for the latest value.
blocks.title: Interview answer
Key points
blocks.text:
- Effects synchronise with outside systems
- Events belong in handlers
- Always clean up
- List all dependencies honestly

### useMemo and useCallback

`useMemo` caches a calculated value, and `useCallback` caches a function, both until dependencies change.

blocks.title: Two genuine reasons to use them

blocks.text:
They aren't free, and don't speed up everything. Without `memo()` on the child, a stable callback changes nothing. Part 9 covers when they're worthwhile. The **React Compiler** adds this memoisation automatically at build time, so such hand-written code is becoming less necessary in projects that use it.

### useReducer

When state changes in many related ways, put all the transitions in one place, as a pure function.

blocks.title: A shopping cart

blocks.text:
A reducer is plain code, so you can unit test it without React. It works like a small state machine.

### useContext

Context passes a value to everything below, without prop drilling.

blocks.title: Authentication through context

blocks.text:
Every consumer renders again when the value changes. Part 6 covers when that's a problem.

### Newer hooks

| Hook | Use |
|---|---|
| `useId` | Stable unique IDs for labels and ARIA |
| `useTransition` | Mark an update as non-urgent, to keep typing smooth |
| `useDeferredValue` | Let a slow part lag behind input |
| `useLayoutEffect` | Measure the DOM before the browser paints |
| `useSyncExternalStore` | Subscribe to an outside store safely |
| `useActionState`, `useOptimistic`, `use` | React 19 form and data patterns |

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- useMemo and useCallback are for real costs
- A reducer gathers transitions in one testable place
- Context avoids prop drilling, but re-renders consumers
- The compiler reduces hand memoisation

A custom hook is a function starting with `use` that calls other hooks. It shares **logic**, not state: each call has its own state.

### Good custom hooks

| Do | Avoid |
|---|---|
| Name by purpose: `useOrders` | Lifecycle wrappers like `useMount` |
| Return what callers need | Hiding effects that surprise callers |
| Keep one concern | One hook that does everything |
| Test it alone | Sharing state by accident |

Test hooks with `renderHook` from Testing Library, as Part 10 shows.
**"Do two components using the same custom hook share state?"** No. Each call gets its own state, because a hook is just a function. To share state, lift it up, use context, or use a store.
blocks.title: Interview answer
Key points
blocks.text:
- Custom hooks share logic, not state
- Clean up timers and listeners
- Handle storage errors
- Name them by purpose

Show the expected result immediately during an action, falling back automatically when it ends.

### useFormStatus

Lets a child know that its parent form is submitting, without passing props.

blocks.title: A submit button anywhere in a form

blocks.text:
It must be in a component **inside** the form, not in the one that renders the form.

### use

`use` reads a promise or context during render, and unlike other hooks, it can be called in conditions.

blocks.title: Reading a promise with Suspense

blocks.text:
The promise must be stable across renders. Creating it during render gives a new one each time, which suspends forever, so create it outside, cache it, or use a framework or library.

blocks.title: Keep the old screen while the next loads

blocks.text:
### The React Compiler

The compiler analyses your components at build time, and adds memoisation, so hand-written `useMemo`, `useCallback` and `memo` are needed less. It needs code that follows the rules of React, so the `react-hooks` ESLint rules matter even more. Existing memoisation doesn't harm, and you can adopt it gradually. It doesn't fix slow calculations in general, oversized bundles or slow APIs.

### Older code you'll still meet

| Older | Modern |
|---|---|
| `forwardRef` | `ref` as a prop |
| `<Context.Provider>` | `<Context>` directly, in React 19 |
| Class lifecycles | Hooks |
| Manual `isSubmitting` state | `useActionState`, `useFormStatus` |

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- useOptimistic reverts when the action ends
- useFormStatus must be inside the form
- use needs a stable promise
- The compiler needs code that follows the rules
#### Rules, useState and useRef

items.question: Why can't a hook go inside an if?
items.answer: React matches hooks by order, so a skipped call shifts every later hook to the wrong slot.

items.question: Would you store a timer ID in useState or useRef?
items.answer: useRef, as it isn't shown, and changing it shouldn't cause a render.

blocks.text: #### useEffect done properly

items.question: A form resets when a prop changes, using an effect. What's cleaner?
items.answer: Give the form a `key` based on that prop, so React recreates it.

items.question: Why might an effect run twice in development?
items.answer: Strict Mode mounts, cleans up and remounts, to test the cleanup. It doesn't in production.

items.question: What goes wrong without aborting a fetch when the id changes?
items.answer: An older response can arrive last and overwrite newer data.

blocks.text: #### useMemo, useCallback and useReducer

items.question: Does useCallback make a component faster by itself?
items.answer: No. It only helps if a memoised child, or a dependency list, relies on the function's identity.

items.question: When would you pick useReducer over useState?
items.answer: When there are many related transitions, or the next state depends on several values. It's also easy to test.

blocks.text: #### Writing custom hooks

items.question: Two components call useDebounce. Do they share the debounced value?
items.answer: No. Each call has its own state.

items.question: Why wrap localStorage in try and catch?
items.answer: It can throw in private modes, when full, or on corrupted JSON. The app should keep working.

items.question: Why debounce search input?
items.answer: To avoid a request per keystroke, and call the API only when typing pauses.

blocks.text: #### The useEffect clinic

items.question: Why does an object created in render make an effect run every time?
items.answer: It's a new reference each render, so the dependency comparison always sees a change.

items.question: Why can't you pass an async function directly to useEffect?
items.answer: It returns a promise, whereas React expects a cleanup function or nothing.

items.question: How do you use the latest callback without reconnecting?
items.answer: Store it in a ref updated each render, and call the ref from a stable effect.

blocks.text: #### React 19: use, Suspense and optimistic UI

items.question: Why must a promise passed to use be stable?
items.answer: A new promise each render suspends again, causing an endless loop of loading.

items.question: Why doesn't useFormStatus work in the component that renders the form?
items.answer: It reads the status of a parent form, so it must be in a child of that form.

items.question: Does the React Compiler make all apps fast?
items.answer: No. It reduces needless re-rendering, but not slow APIs, big bundles or expensive work.
